### Seven Dead on the Railway at Al-Ayyat, the Six of the Square Are Named in Kraków, and Eisenkot Sets His Four Conditions in Jerusalem

Filed as: Edition No. 22 — The Evening Watch · 2026-11-08T18:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-08-evening-watch.html

The Evening File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Seven Dead on the Railway at Al-Ayyat, the Six of the Square Are Named in Kraków, and Eisenkot Sets His Four Conditions in Jerusalem

 The day’s developments whole, at the evening hour: a railway collision south of Cairo supplied the day’s new dead, its toll rising in steps all afternoon; Kraków’s mourning acquired names and ages for its six, a spokesman’s “highly likely” joining the square to the house in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, and a political challenge to the minister who read the attack aloud on Saturday; a drone fell on rescue crews working the worst single bombing of Ukraine’s week; the Gulf file added projectile impacts reported on Qeshm, projectiles reported fired from Sirik, and a gas field halted by a drone in Iraqi Kurdistan; Jerusalem’s mandate-holder published his four conditions and met no coalition; Asunción’s case widened to at least twenty-seven charged while the repayments to savers reached $160 million; and the American count, the quake count apart, ended the day exactly where Friday left it.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1800 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 21, the Midday Watch, collected at 1200 today. Where the evening figures differ from the midday’s, the difference is stated here, in the open. The midday edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Evening in Brief

Sunday evening is a file of tolls revised upward, names supplied, and positions stated for the record, and the desk files it in that order. In Egypt, a train running from Giza to Fayoum struck the rear of a Cairo-to-Aswan train standing in the Al-Ayyat district, and the Health Ministry’s count climbed through the day—four dead and 88 injured in the first official figures, seven dead and 112 injured in the ministry’s later count, with one account carrying 125 injured—in the ministry’s figures as reported through the day filed below. In Kraków, officials identified the six killed in the Main Market Square by age and nationality, prosecutors’ spokesman Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the same person carried out the killings in the square and at the suspect’s home, and the square itself reopened late Sunday, in Reuters’ evening account filed below. In Ukraine, a Russian drone struck the rescue crews at Komyshuvakha, where Monday’s bombing of a former school and a shelter killed at least 55 people and about 50 remain missing. In the Gulf, Iranian media reported projectile impacts on Qeshm Island late Sunday and Iranian state television reported three projectiles launched from Sirik toward vessels; in Iraqi Kurdistan a drone attack halted production at the Khor Mor gas field, in the live file filed below. In Jerusalem, Mr. Eisenkot, mandate in hand, set four conditions for joining his government and challenged the parties that called for unity to form it under him; no faction accepted on Sunday, and no coalition exists. In Asunción, the Ueno case widened—at least 27 people face charges, and the central bank has paid $160 million to nearly 1.2 million savers. In the United States the Senate count did not move at all: Mississippi stands at 2,574 votes on a tally stamped Friday, Alaska at 637, and both wait on Tuesday. That is the evening whole: one new disaster counted, one case named, one mandate conditioned, and a week whose every open question still falls on the same two days, Monday’s handovers and Tuesday’s deadlines.

Al-Ayyat at 1800: Seven Dead on the Railway

The day’s new event happened on the railway south of Cairo, and its numbers are a staircase. Train No. 134, running from Giza to Fayoum, struck the rear of Train No. 2010, running from Cairo to Aswan, between Kafr Ammar and Raqqa stations in the Al-Ayyat district of Giza province, the National Authority for Egyptian Railways said; several carriages left the track and some overturned. The chief prosecutor’s office said its initial inspection found the Giza–Fayoum train had hit the last carriage of the Aswan train, which was stationary on the same track, and that a train conductor was among the dead, in the collated account filed below. The Health Ministry’s first count, carried by the wires at midday, was four dead and 88 injured. By the evening the ministry’s toll stood at seven dead and 112 injured, reported by Sky News and Al Jazeera; a further account of the ministry’s figures carries 125 injured, 132 cases received by hospitals in all, 71 of the injured discharged and 43 still in hospital—23 at Al-Ayyat, 13 at Al-Wasta and 7 at Atfih. Seventy-two ambulances took part in the evacuation. The two injured counts, 112 and 125, are both in the record under the ministry’s name and the desk prints both; the dead, at seven, agree in every later account. President Abdel Fattah al-Sisi ordered an investigation and, in his words, that anyone found to have been negligent be held accountable; the prosecutor general sent a team to examine the site, assess the damage and fix the exact toll; railway crews and cranes were dispatched to clear the line. No cause has been stated by any authority. Al-Ayyat carries a record in this file: a fire on a holiday train there in 2002 killed more than 370 people, the worst disaster on Egypt’s railways. The dead of Sunday have not been named.

Kraków at 1800: The Six Are Named by Age, and the Minister Is Challenged

The mourning acquired its particulars on Sunday. Officials counted the six killed in the Main Market Square as a 51-year-old Austrian woman, a 32-year-old British man, three Polish women aged 47, 53 and 61, and a Polish man of about 50, in the evening brief compiled from the Polish and German reporting filed below; five foreign nationals—from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia—are among the wounded, Reuters reported. The wounded count itself did not settle: 15 in some accounts, 16 in others, and Reuters’ evening wording counts 16 wounded in addition to those killed, including the two police officers and the suspected gunman, who remains in critical condition in hospital. The two officers were woken from drug-induced comas after surgery, the evening brief reports, on the same day the prosecutors announced they had regained consciousness. At the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, the three bodies had gunshot wounds and firearms and a significant quantity of ammunition were recovered from the property, prosecutors’ office spokesperson Daniel Prokopowicz said; it was “highly likely,” he said, that the killings there and in Kraków were carried out by the same person, and the investigations are ongoing. Highly likely is the strongest joining word any official has used, and the desk prints it as a spokesman’s assessment, not a finding. The suspect has still not been questioned, and no charge has been laid.

The day’s considered response in Poland was an argument about the reading, conducted in the open. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said on Saturday that everything points to the attacker having held “very, very radical views” and being “fascinated by far-right ideologies.” The nationalist opposition questioned the grounds: Przemysław Czarnek, deputy head of PiS, wrote that if Mr. Kierwiński “has misinformed the public, he should face political consequences,” and demanded immediate explanations and access to the information the statements rested on. On Sunday the minister declined to retreat: “We are not passing judgement,” he told the broadcaster TVN24. “Always, there are initial hypotheses, information and evidence&hellip; These are things now being checked by the police and I will not elaborate. Nobody is walking anything back.” The desk files the exchange whole: a minister’s hypothesis, an opposition’s demand for its basis, and a refusal to withdraw it, with the investigation that alone can settle the question still running and the man who could answer it unable to speak. The city’s own acts closed the day: the square and its surrounding streets, closed since Saturday, reopened late Sunday; the hourly trumpet call from St. Mary’s tower, suspended for twelve hours overnight, was, the news agency PAP reported, silenced for the first time since 1939; and police tightened security in Warsaw and other cities. National mourning runs through Monday. One figure in this file moved against the paper’s earlier record and the desk states it plainly: the ages of the three found at home are now given as a father of 52 and a mother of 51 in the evening brief, against 53 and 52 in the police statement quoted by Reuters, while the sister stands at 21 in both—and at 20 in the prosecutors’ account the midday edition filed. Three ages, three triangles; the desk chooses in none of them.

Komyshuvakha and Abu Dhabi: A Drone on the Rescuers, and a Table Still Growing

Ukraine’s Sunday entry is a second strike on the site of the week’s worst one. A Russian drone struck emergency workers on rescue missions at Komyshuvakha, near the front line in the Zaporizhzhia region, hitting the former school and the nearby shelter that guided bombs had blasted on Monday as residents waited for humanitarian aid, in the Associated Press account filed below. No one was injured in Sunday’s strike, Ukraine’s State Emergency Service said, but specialized rescue equipment was damaged. The Monday attack’s toll now stands at at least 55 dead, and around 50 people are still listed as missing, Ukraine’s military intelligence agency, HUR, said; many of the bodies recovered have not been identified and DNA analysis is ongoing. HUR said Saturday it had identified some of the Russian service members involved in what it calls the “double tap” strike—the second blow aimed at the same place after the first—and Ukraine has routinely accused Russia of striking the same site in quick succession to target the crews who respond. On Saturday the community buried its dead from the first strike: a farewell ceremony in Zaporizhzhia for six police officers killed at Komyshuvakha, three of them near the former school, and three residents buried near one another where a memorial is planned. No Russian statement on either strike was taken in by the evening. The accounts of both attacks rest on Ukrainian officials and the Associated Press’s reporting from the region; no party that did not issue them has verified the toll.

Two days before the Abu Dhabi table sits, its shape and its claims both grew. France’s confirmation that Europeans will take part acquired its details in the afternoon accounts: Mr. Barrot said he would not personally be at the negotiating table and that Paris had not yet named its representative, in the Euronews account filed below; Russia’s delegation will be led by presidential aide Vladimir Medinsky, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said, in the confirmation account filed below; and the G7 foreign ministers meet in Paris on Monday and Tuesday. The American president’s expectation is also on the record: Mr. Trump predicted a “very big” deal with Russia extending beyond Ukraine to “all of Europe,” in the Associated Press account filed below, and Mr. Barrot said he did not know what the American president had in mind. Russia has suggested there would be no place for European representatives at the table; France says this time they will participate. Both statements stand. No agenda, draft or text has been published by any side, and the talks have not begun.

The Gulf at 1800: Qeshm Again, Projectiles From Sirik, and a Gas Field Halted in Iraq

The strait’s file, which at midday stood at three claimed tanker fires and no names, added reports in both directions on Sunday evening and confirmed none of them. Late in the day, Al Jazeera Arabic cited Iran’s Tasnim agency as reporting that projectiles it attributed to the United States had come down on Qeshm Island, following an earlier report by the state agency IRNA of explosions on the island and sites possibly targeted; American involvement, any damage, and whether the impacts were separate from Saturday’s blasts all remain unverified, in the live file filed below. Iranian state television separately reported that three projectiles were launched from Sirik, on Iran’s southern coast, toward vessels it said were violating Iran’s navigation restrictions; whether any vessel was hit is not established. The Guards’ own statement of the morning, in the Guards’ outlet’s account filed below, holds the three tankers to have exploded and caught fire along an unauthorized route with their systems off, and attributes the burning to the “mischief” of the American army; the second account of the same statement, filed below, notes what the statement does not do—it does not say who caused the explosions and claims no strike by the Guards. No tanker has been named by any party at the evening hour, and the confirmed facts beside the claims stand where the midday edition left them: one rescue of 22 crew by the Emirates, one disabling of the M/V Huda explained by Central Command, neither joined by any authority to the Guards’ tally.

The evening’s one confirmed new fact in the region is in Iraq, and it is an interruption, not an explosion count. A drone attack on Sunday night halted production at the Khor Mor gas field in Sulaymaniyah province, in Iraqi Kurdistan: the drone hit a liquefied petroleum gas storage tank and set it alight, two sources in the regional electricity ministry told Reuters; Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi said an initial assessment found no casualties; the Kurdistan Region’s electricity ministry said the interruption cut gas supplies to five power stations and estimated electricity generation would fall by 2,500 to 2,800 megawatts. No group had claimed responsibility at the evening hour. The land file moved in words at the same time: Mr. Trump said Task Force Iron Gate was operating at full capacity alongside the naval blockade, and the American Treasury has asked Baghdad to close all but two of its border crossings with Iran; Iraq’s foreign minister, Fuad Hussein, said Baghdad was still discussing the request and warned that widespread closures would hurt Iraq’s economy. Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said Tehran’s two-day proposal remained on the table, calling on Washington to accept Iran’s conditions, including an end to the war on all fronts, and warning of retaliation if the United States resumed fighting. Mr. Trump, to CNN, supplied the other half of that exchange: fresh American strikes were “highly unlikely” if negotiations continued to advance, and the United States had identified 38 bridges as potential targets if military action resumed. No agreement has been announced by any party.

The Saudi–Yemen ledger also acquired its evening entries, each with its owner attached. The Saudi-led coalition said it had destroyed two ballistic-missile launchers in Yemen’s Saada region that it said were used in Sunday’s attack on Riyadh. The Houthi military spokesman, Yahya Saree, claimed the movement had hit Riyadh’s financial district and targeted King Khalid International Airport; Saudi authorities did not confirm the airport was hit, and the Energy Ministry attributed the damage to the Aramco Tower to falling debris and reported no casualties there—against witness accounts, filed at midday, of broken glass on several floors and part of a facade torn away. The Houthis’ tally of coalition attacks in Yemen over the previous 24 hours stands at 91 in the evening’s live file and at 105, with six operations of their own claimed against Saudi sites, in the second account filed below; the two tallies are both the movement’s, taken at different hours, and neither has been verified. The Sanaa figure itself did not move: the Houthi-run health ministry’s count for Saturday’s strikes on homes near the capital stands at at least 33 killed, among them eight women and thirteen children, and 39 wounded, with Saudi Arabia’s Center for International Communication saying it was investigating the report. Three officials told the Associated Press that Syria was preparing to send fighters to Saudi Arabia for a possible deployment along the Saudi side of the border with Yemen, an initial contingent of about 600 by one official’s account; a Syrian source had told state media on Saturday that Damascus had no plans to send troops into Yemen and described its cooperation with Riyadh as training and capacity-building. Both statements are in the file; neither has been acted on in any report taken in.

Jerusalem at 1800: Four Conditions, and the First Meetings Set

The mandate’s first evening produced conditions, not a coalition. After receiving the mandate at the 5 p.m. ceremony, Mr. Eisenkot said he would approach all Knesset factions and set four conditions for joining his government: accepting Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, upholding the values of its Declaration of Independence, supporting universal military, national or civilian service, and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation, in the live file filed below. He challenged Likud and Religious Zionism—the parties of the prime minister he would replace and of the unity government Mr. Netanyahu proposed on Saturday—to back a government under his leadership if they stood by their calls for unity. No answer from either party was taken in by the evening. The week’s meetings are set: Mr. Eisenkot was expected to meet Naftali Bennett on Sunday evening and Avigdor Liberman on Monday. The Joint List told the broadcaster N12 it was willing to help end Mr. Netanyahu’s tenure without demanding a place in the government or the coalition, and that it had not yet been asked to commit to voting for an Eisenkot government. The arithmetic stands as the midday edition printed it: the four-party change bloc holds 48 of 120 seats, the Arab-led lists 19 between them, 61 are required, and the clock runs 28 days from today.

The argument that will decide the arithmetic was joined on Sunday, and it is the conscription argument. Mr. Liberman’s stated position, from Friday, is that he is prepared for “painful compromises”—including on the conscription law—to build a coalition of 61 without the Arab lists, and that he has not abandoned conscription, in the account of his announcement filed below. The assessment against it was filed Sunday afternoon: the commentator Amit Segal argued that the price of an arrangement among Liberman, Eisenkot, Bennett and the ultra-Orthodox parties was already established—the ultra-Orthodox would not be drafted—in the afternoon file filed below. The other stated positions stand against any such price: the Democrats’ chairman, Yair Golan, wrote that a genuine partnership requires mutual responsibility and that the ultra-Orthodox must be drafted; the chief executive of Mr. Bennett’s party told its activists that silence does not imply consent, and restated the goal of a revolution in military service. The desk files the positions without choosing among them: a compromise offered, a price assessed, a draft demanded, and a silence that its owner says is not consent. The first test is Monday’s meeting.

Asunción at 1800: Twenty-Seven Charged, and $160 Million Paid Back

Paraguay’s file on its second day is a file of scale: the case’s width and the repayments’ width, printed side by side. At least 27 people face criminal charges in connection with the Ueno collapse, including the bank’s lead shareholder, Miguel Vazquez; former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo is charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain, in addition to the counts he shares with the former president; and each of Mr. Peña’s two charges—breach of trust and administration for personal gain—could carry a sentence of up to ten years, prosecutor Nancy Salomón said, in the evening account published at 15:39 ET and filed below. The sums are now in the record: Ueno administered around $850 million in public money, including roughly $355 million in state pension funds, on the Reuters figures the account carries; the public and social-security funds it held in September 2026 are put at about 3.6 trillion guaraníes, with $163.8 million of the Itaipú hydroelectric dam’s funds among them, in the wire account and the evening brief filed below. The central bank began liquidation proceedings on November 2 after the bank’s solvency ratio fell to less than half the required minimum, and intervened the next day. On the other side of the ledger, the repayment has begun at scale: the central bank said $160 million had been paid to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee scheme, small depositors first, in sums up to 10 million guaraníes—about $1,600—with larger claims to be covered gradually, and banks opened weekend branches to serve customers. The state oil company Petropar has filed a complaint seeking protection for its assets. Mr. Peña declined to testify at Saturday’s hearing; his lawyer, Ricardo Preda, maintains the plea of not guilty and his own forecast of the case: “We will submit to the investigation and I am sure that when this investigation is over the result will be the dismissal.” The opposition’s stated position is Senator Yolanda Paredes’s: the former president “must go, but not home. He must go to a maximum-security prison.” He remains, on the judge’s order, at the Presidential Escort Regiment. President Pedro Alliana is naming a new cabinet to serve through 2028. The charges are charges; no court has ruled on any part of the case, and the presumption of innocence is printed with them.

Washington at 1800: The Handover Comes Monday, and the Responses Are In

The White House change announced on Friday takes effect on Monday, and Sunday was the day the considered responses were filed. Stephen Miller, 41, deputy chief of staff for policy and the president’s homeland security adviser, becomes chief of staff on November 9; Susie Wiles, who gave the president her resignation on Thursday night and whose last day in the post was Friday, moves to the Trump Political Operation, in the account of the announcement filed below. The president’s words on his choice are in the record: “Stephen’s been with me since the beginning. He gets it,” and, departing the White House on Friday, “Stephen’s been great, and sometimes in life, you gotta make moves.” The Senate Democratic leader’s answer supplies the opposition’s reading in one sentence, as the account’s headline carries it: Senator Chuck Schumer’s verdict is that Mr. Trump “has learned nothing from his historic defeat.” From inside the president’s own party, Representative Marlin Stutzman of Indiana, whose vote share fell from 65 percent in 2024 to under 55 this year, called the promotion a mistake: “If your team takes a beating as badly as we took this last week, you have to fire people,” in the evening brief filed below. The reading from Paris, filed Friday, is that the appointment is a doubling down—a retreat into the inner circle after a majority of voters punished the president’s choices at the midterms. The desk files the four readings without adopting one: the president’s loyalty, the opposition’s verdict, a congressman’s dissent from his own side, and an ally-capital’s interpretation. What is not in dispute is the sequence—a resignation offered Thursday night, an announcement Friday, a handover Monday. The Federal Register published nothing on November 7 or November 8, in the Sunday situation report filed below; the weekend’s Washington record is personnel and statements, and the desk files it as such.

The Count at 1800: Frozen at Friday’s Figures, the Estimates Widen

Neither Senate race moved on Sunday, and the correction this watch owes is that nothing has moved since Friday evening. Mississippi’s tally stands where it stood at midday: Scott Colom, the Democrat, at 467,930 votes to the incumbent Republican Cindy Hyde-Smith’s 465,356—a margin of 2,574 on 953,314 counted, 97 percent of the estimated total—and the Sunday situation report, filed below, dates that tally precisely: it is stamped 5:02 p.m. on Friday, November 6, and the results page updated at 3:16 a.m. ET on Sunday shows the same two totals, so no votes have been posted since Friday evening. What moved on Sunday is the estimate of what remains, and the estimates do not agree: the state Republican chairman, Mike Hurst, told CNN that between 23,000 and 25,000 affidavit or mail-in ballots were outstanding, a wider figure than the 10,000 to 15,000 provisional ballots carried on Saturday and wider than the roughly 3,139 mail ballots the Sunday video roundup counts as outstanding. The desk prints the three figures with their owners and chooses in none of them; the calendar is the settled part—mailed ballots must be received, and affidavit voters must cure a missing identification, by 5 p.m. on Tuesday, November 10, counties certify by November 13, Mississippi law provides no recount for this race, and a plurality wins. Alaska stands at 637 first-choice votes, Mary Peltola ahead of Dan Sullivan at 48.2 percent to 47.9 with about 74 percent counted; the next count is expected Monday or Tuesday, and the ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18 if no candidate clears 50 percent. The ledgers above the two races stand at 252 Democrats to 161 Republicans in the House, with 22 House races uncalled, and 54 to 44 in the Senate, in the Associated Press ledger the Sunday report reads. The prediction market’s prices, printed as the venue’s and not the desk’s, put Mr. Colom at 99.0 percent and Ms. Peltola at 98.6—a forecast standing beside a frozen count. At 1800 on the fifth day after the election, neither race has been called.

Shizuoka at 1800: The Count of the Hurt Settles at 22

Central Japan’s correction file, which at midday ran from 15 to 24 injured, settled in the afternoon reports. The afternoon official reports list 19 injured in Aichi Prefecture—one serious injury and 18 minor—and three minor injuries in Shizuoka, 22 in all, in the afternoon account filed below; the television count carried in the second file below gives the same division, 19 in Aichi including one serious case and three in Shizuoka, where an 80-year-old woman fell in Hamamatsu’s Hamana Ward. The morning’s lower figure, 15, was the count of an assessment in its first hours; the 24 carried by some accounts remains in the record as the highest figure printed, and the afternoon official division is the one the desk carries forward. The earthquake itself stands as filed: magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency, 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, at 1:04 a.m. local time beneath western Shizuoka at about 40 kilometres’ depth, upper 5 on the Japanese scale in Chita, Aichi, no tsunami threat and no deaths reported. The agency’s Sunday acts are also in the file: having regard to loosened ground, it lowered the thresholds for issuing landslide warnings for the municipalities of Aichi that shook hardest, and its standing guidance—caution for about a week against tremors up to upper 5, the risk highest in the next two to three days, and its assessment that this quake’s pattern is unlikely to lead to the Nankai Trough megaquake—stands unrevised. A second, separate tremor, magnitude 4.3 in the Kumamoto area at 10:53 a.m., produced no reports of serious damage or injury. Particulars of the hurt are in the accounts: in Tokoname a woman in her fifties was taken to hospital with a fractured ankle; in Toyota a man in his forties and a woman in her eighties fell and struck their heads and were conscious in hospital. The sleeper train Sunrise Izumo made a temporary stop; none of its approximately 290 passengers was reported hurt.

The Markets’ Reading: Friday’s Board, and a Monday That Must Reprice the Weekend

There was no American or European session on Sunday, so the desk prints the board the weekend leaves and the questions Monday must answer. Friday’s close stands as the Sunday situation report carries it: the S&P 500 at 7,376.86, up 0.31 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 24,579.425, up 1.09 percent; the Dow Jones Industrial Average at 51,285.73, down 0.46 percent; and the VIX at 25.64, down 9.01 percent. The ten-year Treasury yielded 4.859 percent; gold’s last print was $4,079.50. Oil’s settlements stand where the midday edition printed them—Brent at $98.32 a barrel, West Texas Intermediate at $90.83—on a week that took about 13 percent off the barrel on the desk’s baseline and about 17 percent on the Sunday newsletter’s, the disagreement filed at midday and unrevised here. The one Sunday session in the file, India’s seventy-minute Diwali Muhurat sitting, closed up 400 points on the Sensex. What Monday holds is a list, not a forecast: the first full session since three tanker fires were claimed in the strait and a drone halted a gas field that feeds five power stations; a chief of staff taking office in Washington; coalition meetings in Jerusalem; and, on Tuesday, the Abu Dhabi talks and the counting deadlines in two American states. The steepest Friday move in the file is Tokyo’s: the Nikkei 225 fell 5.96 percent on Friday, the evening brief notes. Monday’s open is the first price the weekend’s claims will meet.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point. On Al-Ayyat, the dead agree at seven in every later account and the injured stand at 112 in the ministry’s later count and 125 in another account of the ministry’s figures; the desk carries the seven and prints both injured figures. On Kraków, the wounded stand at 15 or 16 by the hour and the source; the three at home stand at 52, 51 and 21 in the evening brief, at 53, 52 and 21 in the police statement, and the sister at 20 in the prosecutors’; the joining of the two crime scenes stands at a spokesman’s “highly likely”; and the minister’s reading stands as a hypothesis its author declines to withdraw and its critics demand he document. On Hormuz, three tanker fires are claimed by the force that polices the route, one projectile report on Qeshm is attributed by one agency to the United States and confirmed by no one, three projectiles from Sirik are reported by a state broadcaster with no hit established, and the one confirmed interruption of the evening is a gas field in Iraq stopped by a drone nobody has claimed. On Riyadh, the damage is debris in the ministry’s account and torn facade in the witnesses’, and the Houthis’ own tally of the coalition’s attacks stands at 91 in one file and 105 in another. On the count, the margins are Friday’s and the outstanding-ballot estimates run from about three thousand to twenty-five thousand depending on who is counting what. On Shizuoka, the hurt settled at 22 in the afternoon official division, between a morning 15 and a printed 24. On Jerusalem, a mandate has been exercised in words—four conditions, published on its first evening—and no government exists. On Asunción, the detention is a fact, the charges are allegations carrying stated penalties, the repayments are a central bank’s figures, and the presumption of innocence is printed with them. The edition closes at 1800 with everything of consequence in this file falling on the same two days: Monday’s handovers and meetings, and Tuesday’s talks and deadlines.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-eight items.

 

 SubjectiveReuters — Poland mourns the victims of the Kraków mass shooting as security fears growKRAKOW, Nov 8: Poland began two days of national mourning on Sunday and police bolstered security after six people were killed in the southern city’s historic main square, an attack the government said was likely inspired by far-right ideology, following a string of October school stabbings officials linked to extremist content online. Sixteen people were wounded in addition to those killed, including two police officers and the suspected gunman, a 24-year-old Polish man who remained in critical condition in hospital. One of the dead was a British citizen and another Austrian; five foreign nationals, from Austria, Britain, Germany, Portugal and Russia, were among the wounded. Prosecutor’s office spokesperson Daniel Prokopowicz said it was “highly likely” the killings in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski and Kraków were carried out by the same person, and that the three bodies at the home had gunshot wounds, with firearms and a significant quantity of ammunition recovered from the property. Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński’s Saturday reading drew a demand from PiS deputy head Przemysław Czarnek for explanations and the information behind it; on Sunday the minister told TVN24 he was not retracting his statements and that the motive investigation was ongoing. The square and surrounding streets reopened late Sunday; the hourly trumpet call from St Mary’s was suspended for twelve hours, the first time since 1939, PAP reported; police tightened security in Warsaw and other cities; and the two wounded officers have regained consciousness.

 SubjectiveAAP — Poland in mourning after the Kraków mass shootingPoland has begun two days of national mourning after a 24-year-old man with far-right views drove into the busy central square in Kraków and opened fire, killing six people and wounding 15 others before police shot and wounded him; the defence minister described the attack as an “act of terror.” By Saturday evening mourners had left candles, the square remained partially closed on Sunday morning as the investigation continued, and St Mary’s Trumpet Call was paused overnight in tribute. Authorities found the bodies of the assailant’s sister, mother and father at the family home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski; flags were lowered to half-mast; prosecutors have opened an investigation into murder and attempted murder, including of police officers, as an act constituting a terrorist offence; and four women and two men were killed in the square shooting.

 SubjectiveIsrael Realtime — Eisenkot to receive the mandate; rival coalition plans take shapePublished November 8 at 3:59 p.m. Israel time: President Isaac Herzog invited Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to the President’s Residence to formally receive the mandate to form a government on Sunday, November 8, at 5 p.m. Israel time, the announcement issued Saturday evening following Thursday’s consultations and weekend discussions with leaders including Prime Minister Netanyahu and Eisenkot. Factions representing 67 Knesset members recommended Eisenkot, 46 recommended Netanyahu, and a faction representing seven declined to recommend anyone; the recommendations are separate from competing proposals for a government’s composition. Once assigned, Eisenkot has 28 days, with presidential extensions totalling up to 14 more. Under the Basic Law, if he presents a government and the Knesset rejects its request for confidence, the decision on the next stage returns to the president; the mandate also determines which faction supplies the chair of the Knesset’s Arrangements Committee. Yisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Liberman announced he was willing to compromise on conscription legislation and form a government with the ultra-Orthodox parties; Eisenkot’s proposed alternative, in this account, is a minority government of 48 seats supported externally by the Arab parties, potentially with United Torah Judaism abstaining.

 SubjectiveIsrael Realtime — conscription: Segal’s assessment, Bennett’s party and GolanPublished November 8 at 5:16 p.m. Israel time: the commentator Amit Segal argued that Liberman’s rejection of reliance on the Arab parties had undermined Eisenkot’s minority-government plan before Eisenkot formally received the mandate, and that the promise to draft the ultra-Orthodox had vanished from the opening positions, the price of an arrangement involving Liberman, Eisenkot, Bennett and the ultra-Orthodox parties already established—the ultra-Orthodox would not be drafted—which he portrayed as a victory for Rabbi Landau; that assessment differs from Liberman’s stated position that he has not abandoned conscription. Segal also reported Liberman was giving up on appointing Yair Lapid as Knesset speaker, leaving Eisenkot or Bennett as the alternatives. Bruria Naim Arman, chief executive of Bennett’s Together party, told activists that silence does not imply consent and restated the goal of a Zionist government of reform that would implement a revolution in military service; Segal questioned whether a government formed with Arab-party votes would meet the former condition and said Bennett had not agreed to Liberman’s proposed arrangement and was not expected to. Democrats chairman Yair Golan wrote that his party wants a partnership with the ultra-Orthodox community, but a genuine partnership requires mutual responsibility, and that ultra-Orthodox Jews must be drafted into the military.

 SubjectiveAll Israel News — paving the way to a surprise coalition? Liberman announces support for a government with an ultra-Orthodox party and the Eisenkot blocYisrael Beiteinu chairman Avigdor Liberman publicly announced his support on Friday for forming a coalition with the ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism, soon receiving backing from The Democrats and UTJ, though it remains unclear whether the other Change Bloc members who campaigned on a strict new draft law will agree. For the bloc to reach 61 seats it would need to add both UTJ’s seven and Shas’s six to its own 48; UTJ has publicly broken with the prime minister, while Shas supported Netanyahu. Liberman appeared to backtrack on his longstanding demand for harsh penalties for draft dodgers, arguing a government is needed quickly to “prevent the destruction” of the Jewish state; he criticised Eisenkot for past decisions, ruled out a rotation agreement for the premiership, and declared himself prepared for “painful compromises” on three conditions—ending the “Netanyahu era,” preventing new elections, and ruling out a minority government relying on the abstention of the Joint List and Ra’am—adding: “On all other issues, it is permissible and desirable to be flexible and compromise&hellip; this includes the issue of the conscription law. This pains me, and I know it pains many others as well.” Eisenkot had reportedly been more interested in a minority government relying on outside Arab-party support; his party said Thursday it planned to form “a national emergency government&hellip; immediately.” Updated November 8.

 SubjectiveNationWire — Paraguay’s ex-president Peña jailed in the bank probePublished November 8 at 15:39 ET: Judge Humberto Otazú ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at the Presidential Escort Regiment after prosecutors charged him with breach of trust and administration for personal gain; Peña, 47, was questioned for about three hours on Saturday and declined to testify at the hearing, his lawyer Ricardo Preda maintaining the plea of not guilty: “We will submit to the investigation and I am sure that when this investigation is over the result will be the dismissal.” Each charge could carry up to ten years, prosecutor Nancy Salomón said. At least 27 people face charges, including Ueno’s lead shareholder Miguel Vazquez; former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo is charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and administration for personal gain, and headed the lender until 2023 before becoming its regulator. Ueno administered around $850 million in public money, including roughly $355 million in state pension funds; the central bank began liquidation on November 2 after the solvency ratio fell below half the required minimum and intervened on November 3. The Chamber of Deputies voted 78–0 to impeach and the Senate removed Peña 44–0 with one absent; removal stripped him of the lifetime Senate seat and immunity of a former president; he is only the second Paraguayan president removed by impeachment, after Fernando Lugo in 2012. The central bank said Saturday that $160 million had been paid to nearly 1.2 million savers under the deposit guarantee scheme. Prosecutors are weighing requests to freeze assets.

 SubjectiveHong Kong Business Wire, carrying AFP — impeached Paraguay leader charged over the bank implosionParaguayan prosecutors charged ex-president Santiago Peña and took him into custody on Saturday over a banking crisis that saw millions cut off from their money and sparked major protests. Peña, Paraguay’s youngest-ever president, was removed by the Senate on Friday, three days after the collapse of a leading bank with which he had business links, and was brought before prosecutors and charged with “breach of trust and mismanagement for personal gain” after about three hours of questioning over his links to Ueno Bank, a digital-first company with which nearly half of Paraguay’s population of 6.5 million have accounts. An indictment states that “between 2023 and 2026, UENO BANK S.A. allegedly received deposits and loans from public and pension entities” and “was also allegedly granting loans to companies linked to the bank’s economic group in an irregular manner.” Peña spent Friday night in custody after being arrested within an hour of his impeachment trial; protesters gathered outside his home to demand he be locked up in a regular prison. He was replaced by former vice president Pedro Alliana, who promised not to abandon the almost three million depositors, including pensioners, affected by Ueno’s demise; thousands had taken to the streets demanding their money back after the central bank took control of Ueno, citing fears for its solvency.

 SubjectiveUSA Today — Trump names Stephen Miller the new chief of staff, replacing Susie WilesWASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said top aide Stephen Miller will replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff, a dramatic staff shake-up days after Republicans suffered historic losses in the midterm election, and the most significant White House personnel move of his second term. The 41-year-old Miller, a deputy chief of staff, will begin as chief of staff on November 9, while Wiles moves to the president’s political operation. The overhaul comes after Wiles became a target of Steve Bannon and other MAGA allies after Republicans lost control of the House and Senate; Wiles, 69, previously worked on Trump’s three campaigns before being tapped as chief of staff. The account carries the opposition’s reading in its section heading: “Schumer: ‘Trump has learned nothing from his historic defeat.’”

 SubjectiveDaily Caller — Trump taps top immigration adviser as new chief of staffPresident Donald Trump has tapped top immigration adviser Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff, his announcement coming three days after Republicans lost both chambers of Congress in Tuesday’s midterms. In a post on Truth Social on Friday, the president announced that Miller will fill the position starting Monday and thanked the current chief of staff: “I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026. Susie Wiles, who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation. I want to thank her for her service as Chief of Staff—She has done a great job.” Following the announcement, Wiles confirmed in a statement on X that Friday would be her final day, and the Caller confirms that Wiles gave the president her resignation on Thursday night. Miller has served as deputy chief of staff for policy and homeland security adviser since January 2025, and posted on X on Friday: “It has been the privilege of my lifetime to have served on his team from Day One, and I am honored beyond words to serve as his White House Chief of Staff.”

 SubjectiveHuffman Writes — SITREP: November 8, 2026The Sunday situation report: in Mississippi the count did not move at all—the tally stood at 2,574 votes on 953,314 counted, stamped 5:02 p.m. on Friday, with mailed and affidavit ballots due or curable by 5 p.m. on Tuesday; the results page updated at 3:16 a.m. ET on November 8 shows the same totals, so no votes have been posted since Friday evening; the state Republican chairman, Mike Hurst, told CNN that between 23,000 and 25,000 affidavit or mail-in ballots were outstanding. The congressional ledgers did not move over the weekend: the Associated Press ledger read 252 Democrats to 161 Republicans in the House with 22 races uncalled, and 54 to 44 in the Senate with two uncalled. Polymarket priced Colom at 99.0 percent and Peltola at 98.6—the venue’s prices, not the report’s view. The Federal Register published nothing on November 7 or 8; the Supreme Court and the D.C. Circuit filed no opinions in the window. The board is Friday’s close: the S&P 500 at 7,376.86, up 0.31 percent; the Nasdaq Composite at 24,579.425, up 1.09 percent; the Dow at 51,285.73, down 0.46 percent; the VIX at 25.64, down 9.01 percent; the ten-year Treasury at 4.859 percent; gold’s last print $4,079.50. On Israel, the report notes the mandate went to the man with fewer seats—Netanyahu’s camp 53, the opposition bloc 48, Likud the largest single party at 27—and that the Arab parties won a record 19 between them.

 SubjectiveSenate Watch, on YouTube — Senate update, November 8: what changed in Mississippi, Alaska and the leadership fightsThe Sunday roundup, one chapter per story, its figures as of the dates shown on screen and campaign claims labelled as claims: Mississippi—Democrat Scott Colom leads Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by 2,574 votes, 49.1 percent to 48.8, with about 97 percent counted on the Associated Press count posted Friday evening, his lead grown from 1,138 on Thursday morning; about 3,139 mail ballots were outstanding as of Friday and count if they arrive by Tuesday, November 10; affidavit ballots are still being reviewed and estimates of how many remain vary; counties must certify by November 13 and Mississippi has no recount process. Alaska—Democrat Mary Peltola leads Senator Dan Sullivan by 637 first-choice votes with about 74 percent counted, on a count posted Wednesday; the next count is expected November 9 or 10 and a ranked-choice tabulation is set for November 18 if no one tops 50 percent. The Associated Press has Democrats at 54 seats and Republicans at 44, so Democrats take control on January 3; the two open races decide whether the majority is 54, 55 or 56.

 SubjectiveThe Gold Standard — the Japan quake injures people in Aichi and ShizuokaA magnitude 5.7 earthquake shook central Japan early on Sunday, injuring people in Aichi and Shizuoka prefectures. Afternoon official reports list one serious injury and 18 minor injuries in Aichi, and three minor injuries in Shizuoka—22 in all. Japan’s weather agency said no tsunami was expected and warned of more strong shaking over the week after the quake. Published Sunday, November 8, 2026, at 8:48 p.m. Adelaide time.

 SubjectiveTV Asahi News, on YouTube — a large tremor before dawn: maximum intensity upper 5 in the Tokai region, 22 injuredAn earthquake with a maximum intensity of upper 5 struck the Tokai region in the early hours of November 8, injuring 22 people in various locations, including those who fell. According to the Japan Meteorological Agency the earthquake occurred at about 1:04 a.m. with its epicentre in western Shizuoka Prefecture, registering upper 5 in Chita City, Aichi Prefecture. In Aichi Prefecture 19 injuries have been confirmed, including one serious case; in Shizuoka Prefecture three people were injured, including an 80-year-old woman who fell, in Hamana Ward, Hamamatsu City, where an intensity of lower 5 was observed. The Sunrise Izumo sleeper train made a temporary stop, but none of its approximately 290 passengers was reported unwell or injured.

### Prosecutors Open the Kraków Case as a Terrorist Offence, a Third Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, and the Mandate Is Handed Over in Jerusalem

Filed as: Edition No. 21 — The Midday Watch · 2026-11-08T12:00:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/editions/2026-11-08-midday-watch.html

The Midday File — The Desk’s Report

 Objective

 Prosecutors Open the Kraków Case as a Terrorist Offence, a Third Tanker Is Claimed in Hormuz, and the Mandate Is Handed Over in Jerusalem

 The news at midday on a mourning Sunday: the Kraków case acquired its legal shape in the morning—an investigation opened, a terrorist-offence classification, six murder charges in preparation and possibly nine—while its human counts still disagreed by one in three places. In the Gulf, the Guards’ tanker tally grew from two to three without a single ship being named, and Tehran answered Washington’s new land-routes task force in one word. In Jerusalem the mandate changed hands at 5 p.m. as scheduled. In Paris the Abu Dhabi table acquired European chairs. The count did not move. The markets, closed in America and Europe, read the weekend off Friday’s settlements and one festive hour in Mumbai.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1200 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026. This edition continues the log from Edition No. 19, the Overnight Watch, collected at 0400 today, and from Special Report No. 4, filed at 0910 today. Where the midday figures differ from the morning’s, the difference is stated here, in the open. The overnight edition stands unrevised, as a log stands.

The Midday in Brief

Sunday at noon is a file of openings and standings, and the desk files it in that order. In Kraków, on the first day of Poland’s national mourning, prosecutors opened the formal investigation the overnight edition left unopened: the Saturday attack is classified as a terrorist offence, the investigation covers two acts—the murder of six people in the Main Market Square and the murder of three people at the suspect’s home in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski—and prosecutors are preparing six murder charges that could rise to nine if the same hand is established for the three at home, in the prosecutors’ Sunday statement filed below. The suspect has not been formally arrested, because his condition in hospital does not allow it; he is under constant surveillance, and no motive has been established. In Jerusalem, the mandate the night announced was handed over: President Isaac Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot the task of forming Israel’s next government at the ceremony set for 5 p.m. local time, 1000 ET, on the strength of 67 recommendations against 46 for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu; Mr. Eisenkot has 28 days, and no coalition exists. In the Strait of Hormuz, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards raised their own tally in the morning from two tankers burning to three, still naming none of them, and their spokesman dismissed the American Task Force Iron Gate, announced Saturday, as wordplay. In Paris, Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said Europeans will be represented at Tuesday’s talks in Abu Dhabi, which had been presented until Sunday as a trilateral table. The Senate count did not move: Mississippi stands at 2,574 votes and Alaska at 637 in the Sunday-morning tallies, and both counts speak next on Tuesday. The markets are closed in the United States and Europe; the Sunday reading is Friday’s settlements—Brent at $98.32, West Texas Intermediate at $90.83—and India’s one-hour Diwali session, which closed up. That is the whole of the midday record: a case opened, a mandate handed over, a tally raised without names, a table enlarged, a count standing, and a week waiting on Tuesday.

Kraków at 1200: Prosecutors Open the Case

The morning’s completed act in Poland is a legal one. A prosecutor of the Małopolska Branch of the National Prosecutor’s Office for Organised Crime and Corruption has commenced an investigation into Saturday’s attack, classified under terrorist offences, spokesman Tomasz Waszczuk announced, in the statement carried by the Polish news agency and filed below. The investigation covers two distinct acts: the murder of six people with a firearm in the square, with the attempted murder of others including police officers on duty, and the murder of the three people in Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski. Prosecutor General Waldemar Żurek noted that the division handles cases related to terrorist crimes and that both acts carry the potential penalty of life imprisonment. Mr. Waszczuk told ABC News that prosecutors are preparing six murder charges, potentially rising to nine if investigators establish that the gunman was also responsible for the deaths of his parents and sister, in the second account filed below. The three at home were found with bullet wounds, the police spokesman said, so it is likely they died of gunshot wounds; likely is the word in the record, and no finding has been made. The suspect himself has not yet been formally arrested, because his medical condition required hospital transport; he remains under constant surveillance and cannot yet be questioned, and prosecutors say that may not be possible for hours or days. One fact of care arrived with the legal file: both injured police officers have regained consciousness, the spokesman confirmed.

The corrections the midday watch exists to print are in this case, and the desk prints them as disagreements, not as choices. The wounded count does not agree across the Sunday files: the prosecutors’ statement carries 16 injured, including the two officers; the morning accounts from the square carry 15. The overnight edition carried both figures in its own files and printed the disagreement; at noon it stands unresolved. The suspect’s age does not agree either: the prosecutors and the police give 24, as this paper has filed him, while several Sunday accounts give 25, and one gives a birth year, 2002, that supports neither cleanly. The age of the sister found dead at home does not agree: the accounts the overnight edition relied on gave 21, following the police confirmation; the prosecutors’ account filed this morning gives 20, for a father of 53 and a mother of 52 on whom all accounts agree. The desk does not round a disputed fact into print; it publishes the triangle. What is settled at noon is the shape of the case: nine dead in one investigation, six in a public square and three in a private house, a terrorist-offence classification, an interior minister’s reading of radical, ultra-nationalist views that remains a reading, and a country in the first of two days of national mourning, with a Mass for the victims set for 4 p.m. local time at St. Mary’s Basilica and Kraków’s own mourning running through November 11. No motive has been established by any investigator, and no charge has yet been laid against a man who cannot be questioned.

Jerusalem at 1200: The Mandate Is Handed Over

The ceremony the night announced took place on its schedule. President Herzog was to hand the mandate to Mr. Eisenkot at 5 p.m. Sunday at the President’s Residence in Jerusalem—1000 ET, two hours before this edition collected—and the live file filed below heads its 5:07 p.m. Cyprus-time entry, 1007 ET, with the handover itself: Herzog hands Eisenkot the mandate to form Israel’s next government. The arithmetic under the ceremony stands as the overnight edition filed it. Factions representing 67 of the Knesset’s 120 members recommended Mr. Eisenkot, against 46 for Mr. Netanyahu, with United Torah Judaism’s seven recommending neither; the 67 are not a coalition—they are 48 members of Mr. Eisenkot’s four-party change bloc and 19 from the Arab-led parties, whose support as formal partners Mr. Eisenkot has ruled out, in the account filed below. The October 27 election gave Mr. Netanyahu’s bloc 53 seats and the change bloc 48, neither at the 61 required. Mr. Eisenkot’s own statement, posted Saturday evening, is on the record: “Now is the time for the formation of a national emergency government,” and, “I will do everything to make us worthy.” Mr. Netanyahu’s answer, in a video statement the same evening, urged the change-bloc parties to form a national unity government that must include his previous coalition allies—a prospect the accounts describe as unlikely. Mr. Netanyahu remains prime minister while the formation proceeds. The clock is now the fact: 28 days from today, with a presidential extension of up to 14 days possible, and no agreement of any kind announced by noon.

Hormuz at 1200: Two Tankers Become Three, and Iron Gate Is Answered

The Guards’ tally grew in the morning, and nothing else about it changed. The Revolutionary Guards Navy announced on Sunday that three oil tankers had exploded and caught fire in the Strait of Hormuz after travelling on a route it declares off-limits, raising the tally it gave in the night—two tankers, struck on mines, one east of the strait and one within it—by one, in the live file and in the Guards’ own outlet’s account, both filed below. The third fire’s cause is not separately stated; no tanker is named, no flag is given, and no crew is accounted for, by the Guards or by anyone else. The neighbouring facts stand unjoined, as the desk filed them at 0400: the United Arab Emirates National Guard rescued all 22 crew, all Arab nationals and all stable, from a burning cargo ship in the Gulf of Oman that it did not name; the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations agency reported a tanker on fire Saturday about eight nautical miles northwest of Khasab, Oman, its crew evacuated; and United States Central Command identified the ship its aircraft disabled in the same waters on Saturday as the St. Kitts and Nevis-flagged cargo ship M/V Huda, struck in the stern with precision munitions after its crew ignored repeated warnings and tried to run the naval blockade, in the morning account filed below. No authority has linked any of these three reports to any other, and the desk does not link them. Three fires claimed, one rescue confirmed, one disabling explained, zero tanker names published: that is the strait at noon.

The war of statements supplied the rest of the Gulf file. Central Command announced on Saturday a new unit, Task Force Iron Gate—about 20 civilian and military personnel in Tampa, Florida, directed by Admiral Brad Cooper to monitor, detect, and disrupt the movement of advanced weapons, dual-use technology, sanctioned materials, and illegal revenue across Iran’s land borders and the Caspian Sea, in the task force account filed below. On Sunday the Guards’ spokesman, Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi, answered it to the Fars agency: “The Iron Gate plan is just wordplay. The Americans cannot achieve their goal of imposing severe economic pressure and causing Iran’s economy to collapse this way.” He added that Washington can never achieve the economic blockade it seeks, whatever form it takes, and warned of a harsher response if the United States attacks Iranian vessels. In the second Gulf theatre, the Saudi-led coalition’s Sunday-morning tally stood at five interceptions—two ballistic missiles toward Riyadh, one toward the Eastern Province, and two cruise missiles in the Riyadh and southern regions—with the Energy Ministry reporting limited debris damage to an Aramco office building in Riyadh’s King Abdullah Financial District and no casualties, in the live file filed below. Qatar’s Foreign Ministry condemned the Houthi attacks in the strongest terms on Sunday, citing the two ballistic missiles toward Riyadh, and called for an immediate halt, in the QNA statement filed below; Bahrain and Syria condemned the attacks as well in the accounts taken in. The other side of that ledger also moved: the authorities in Sanaa raised their toll for Saturday’s strikes on homes in Bani Hushaysh district, near the capital, from 27 killed and 36 wounded to at least 33 killed and 39 wounded. Each figure is printed with its owner; none has been verified by a party that did not issue it.

Abu Dhabi at 1200: Europe Joins the Table

The talks acquired participants on Sunday, two days before they open. Europeans will participate in the talks on Ukraine in Abu Dhabi on Tuesday and Wednesday, November 10 and 11, French Foreign Minister Jean-Noël Barrot said on Sunday, in Reuters’ Paris file filed below: “The Europeans will be well represented; France will be in Abu Dhabi to take part in these discussions. I can’t tell you yet who will be representing France on this occasion, but France will certainly be there.” Mr. Barrot added that no one will speak in Europe’s name without Europe in the room. Until Sunday the meeting had been presented, by the American envoy who announced it and by every capital, as trilateral—Ukraine, Russia, and the United States, the first direct round in months, on post-war security arrangements, de-escalation, and humanitarian questions. Ukraine’s position going in stands as its president stated it Saturday: Russia is intensifying its attacks—36 ballistic missiles and 172 drones in his count of Friday night’s barrage—to lay the groundwork for pressure on Ukraine’s position and its partners’ at the talks, and Russia perceives diplomacy as a form of aggression, in the Arab News account filed below. Mr. Zelenskyy has also said he hopes the round opens the way to a meeting of leaders. No Russian statement taken in by noon answers either the pressure charge or the European chairs. What changed at midday is the table’s shape, not its agenda: no agenda, draft, or text has been published by any side.

Asunción at 1200: The Detention’s Second Day

Paraguay’s file did not move on Sunday, and the desk files it standing, with its papers in order. The detention order of Saturday stands through its second day: Judge Humberto Otazú ordered former President Santiago Peña held in pretrial detention at a military facility—the Presidential Escort Regiment in the local accounts—and former central bank chief Carlos Carvallo held in a detention centre, on charges of breach of trust and administration for personal gain in the investigation of the digital lender Ueno, whose collapse has left millions of customers struggling to access their accounts, in the Reuters account filed below. The judge said detention was necessary to ensure Mr. Peña remained in the country while the case proceeded. Mr. Peña’s attorney, Ricardo Preda, told journalists he is pleading not guilty. Prosecutors are reported to be seeking a freeze of the former president’s assets, a request no ruling taken in by noon has answered. The sequence stands as filed: the central bank resolved Ueno on Tuesday, November 3; the Senate removed Mr. Peña on Friday; Vice President Pedro Alliana holds the presidency for the term through August 2028; the charges were laid and the detention ordered on Saturday. The charges are charges. Mr. Peña is presumed innocent of them, and no court has ruled on any part of the case.

The Count at 1200: The Margins Stand, the Snapshots Are Dated

Neither Senate race moved on Sunday morning, and the correction this watch owes is about dates, not digits. The Sunday-morning tracker, updated at 8:16 a.m. Central, carries Mississippi exactly where the week left it: Scott Colom, the Democrat, at 467,930 votes to Cindy Hyde-Smith’s, the Republican incumbent’s, 465,356—a margin of 2,574 votes, 49.1 percent to 48.8, with about 97 percent of the expected vote counted and roughly 30,498 ballots estimated left, in the two-races account filed below. Alaska stands where it has stood since Wednesday: Mary Peltola, the Democrat, at 102,962 first-choice votes to Dan Sullivan’s, the Republican incumbent’s, 102,325—a margin of 637, with about 74 percent counted and the second candidate named Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. holding 3,600 votes, more than five times the margin. Against those standings, the desk notes a figure in circulation this morning: an explainer on the delays, republished Sunday, carries Mississippi’s margin as 1,138 votes—which was Wednesday night’s margin, in the explainer filed below. Both figures are true of their hours; only one is true of this one. A count is a dated instrument, and the desk dates it. The calendar around the standings is unchanged and triple-headed: on Tuesday, November 10, Mississippi’s mail ballots postmarked by Election Day must arrive and its boards of commissioners complete the provisional count, and Alaska publishes its next update; Mississippi counties certify by November 13; Alaska’s absentee ballots arrive through November 18, when the ranked-choice tabulation is set, no candidate having cleared 50 percent. Colorado’s 4th District stands uncalled with the two Senate races, the Democrat, Eileen Laubacher, ahead by 3,172 votes in Friday’s figures, no newer figure taken in by noon. Democrats hold at least 54 Senate seats whatever the two races decide. At noon on the fifth day, neither race has been called.

Shizuoka at 1200: The Count of the Hurt Settles Into a Range

Central Japan’s morning produced the day’s other correction file: not a new event, but a settling count. The earthquake itself stands as the overnight edition filed it: magnitude 5.7 by the Japan Meteorological Agency, 5.5 by the United States Geological Survey, at 1:04 a.m. local time beneath western Shizuoka Prefecture at a depth of about 40 kilometres, upper 5 on the Japanese intensity scale in Chita, Aichi—the strongest shaking in western Shizuoka in 107 years and in Aichi since 1997—with no tsunami threat and no deaths reported. The injured count rose through the morning and the accounts do not land on one figure. The Seoul account, drawing on the meteorological agency and NHK, counts 15 injured—12 in Aichi, hurt in falls and by blows to the head, and three in Shizuoka, in the morning file filed below. The wire account carried in India counts at least 22 injured, with shattered storefront windows and disrupted trains, in the second file below; local papers and broadcasters in the region have carried 24. The desk publishes the range, 15 to 24, and notes that the counts were taken at different hours of an assessment still under way. The agency’s standing guidance is the settled part: caution for about a week against tremors up to upper 5, the risk highest in the next two to three days, and its assessment that the quake’s pattern differs from, and is unlikely to lead to, the Nankai Trough megaquake.

The Markets’ Reading: Friday’s Settlements, One Festive Hour, and a Monday

There is no American or European session to report on a Sunday, so the desk reports the readings the weekend published. On the settlements, the Sunday accounts agree to the cent: Brent crude closed Friday at $98.32 a barrel and West Texas Intermediate at $90.83, in the Saudi Sunday-morning snapshot and in the Sunday markets newsletter, both filed below, the snapshot noting that Saudi markets open their week on Sunday with those Friday figures as the last confirmed settlements. On the week’s size, the accounts do not agree, and the disagreement is a matter of baselines: the newsletter measures Brent down about 17 percent from $117.64 at the end of the week before; this paper’s Saturday file measured the same barrel down 13.3 percent on the week from its own baseline, and a Sunday market table prints 12.7 percent for Brent and 11.9 for West Texas Intermediate. The settlements are the point; the percentages are the triangle, and the desk prints both. Underneath every measure sits the same fact the newsletter states plainly: expectations of de-escalation in the Iran conflict took the geopolitical premium out of the barrel during the week, and the tanker fires around the Gulf mean the supply risk has not disappeared—a sentence written before the Guards raised their tally to three this morning, and the first thing Monday’s open will reprice.

The one session the world did hold on Sunday was seventy minutes long and festive. India’s exchanges opened for the Diwali Muhurat session—pre-open at 2:05 p.m. in Mumbai, continuous trading from 2:20 to 3:30 p.m., 0350 to 0500 ET—marking Laxmi Pujan and the start of Samvat 2083, the Hindu financial new year. The session closed up: the Sensex rose 400 points to 81,406 and the Nifty crossed 25,100, with Tata Steel and Sun Pharma among the leading gainers, in the session’s account filed below. Regular Indian trading resumes Monday and closes again Tuesday for Diwali-Balipratipada. It is a ceremonial hour and the desk files it as one; its direction, on the day Poland mourned and the strait burned in claims, was up. The rest of the markets’ week is a calendar: Monday’s full reopening, Tuesday’s talks in Abu Dhabi and counting deadlines in two American states, and an oil price that ended Friday below a hundred dollars with a war premium half in and half out.

The Cocked Hat

Three bearings, honestly plotted, give a triangle and not a point. On Kraków, the triangle has three sides: the wounded at 15 in the square accounts and 16 in the prosecutors’; the suspect at 24 in the prosecutors’ and police accounts and 25 in others; his sister at 20 in the morning’s prosecutors’ account and 21 in the accounts the overnight edition filed. The desk publishes all three triangles and chooses in none of them; the settled facts are the investigation, the classification, and the nine dead. On Hormuz, the Guards say three tankers; no name, flag, crew, or independent confirmation attaches to any of the three, and the confirmed rescue and the explained disabling beside them are separate reports that no authority has joined. On Shizuoka, the injured stand between 15 and 24 by the hour of the count, and the magnitude stands at 5.7 by the agency that owns the scale and 5.5 by the American survey. On the count, the margins are unchanged and the figures in circulation are dated Wednesday, Friday, and Sunday; read with their dates, they do not conflict. On oil, the settlements agree and the weekly percentages do not, because their baselines do not. On Jerusalem, the mandate has changed hands and no government has been formed; both halves of that sentence are the news. On Asunción, the detention is a fact and the charges are allegations, and the presumption of innocence is printed with them. The edition closes at noon with the case opened, the mandate running, the table enlarged, the count standing, and everything of consequence in this file—the Abu Dhabi talks, the counting deadlines, the markets’ reopening—falling on the same Tuesday.

 The Clippings Filed With This Edition

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective—a source with a position, printed because it is useful—and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only item in this edition stamped objective. Twenty-four items.

### Deportation in America: Visa Overstays, Removal Orders, and How the Law Actually Works

Filed as: Special Report No. 5 — Filed Outside the Watches · 2026-11-08T11:15:00-05:00 · https://objectivedailynews.com/special-reports/2026-11-08-deportation.html

Special Report

 The Removal File — Status, Process, and the Counts

 Objective

 Deportation in America: Visa Overstays, Removal Orders, and How the Law Actually Works

 Deportation in the United States is an administrative process, not a criminal sentence: being present without status is a civil violation, while entering improperly and reentering after removal are federal crimes, and the system runs on that seam. Its caseload is majority non-criminal in the recent record—two-thirds of fiscal 2024 removals involved no criminal conviction or pending charge—its court backlog stands above three million cases, more than 1.4 million people carry final removal orders unenforced, and the statute that governs it, at the removability stage, asks nothing about whether the person removed is good. The desk files the law, the process, the counts, and the error file, in that order.

 By Eunice, the desk · Collected and analyzed at 1115 ET, Sunday, November 8, 2026.

The File in Brief

The desk has no position on immigration policy in this file, for or against, and this report is written from that position: the law, the process, and the counts, with every side’s claims tested by the same instrument. On the verified record: unlawful presence in the United States is a civil violation, not a crime; improper entry (8 U.S.C. &sect;1325) and reentry after removal (&sect;1326) are crimes; and removal itself is an administrative proceeding under the Immigration and Nationality Act, run through two statute lists—the grounds of inadmissibility at INA &sect;212, applied to people seeking entry, and the grounds of deportability at INA &sect;237, applied to people already admitted. The standard track runs from a notice to appear through master calendar and merits hearings before an immigration judge, with appeal to the Board of Immigration Appeals, and three faster tracks run beside it: expedited removal at the border and, since January 2025, by designation nationwide; administrative removal for aggravated felons without a judge; and reinstatement of an old order without a new hearing. The consequences are tiered by how a person leaves: a removal order carries reentry bars of five, ten, or twenty years under INA &sect;212(a)(9)(A), permanent for aggravated felons, while voluntary departure—taken before or after proceedings conclude, under different conditions—carries no removal-order bar, though the separate three- and ten-year unlawful-presence bars at &sect;212(a)(9)(B) turn on time accrued, not on the manner of leaving. The counts: ICE removed 271,484 people in fiscal 2024, of whom 88,763, or 32.7 percent, had criminal convictions or pending charges; the no-criminal-history share of removals has risen every recent year, reaching roughly two-thirds in 2024 and higher in 2025 by independent reconstruction, and in ICE’s interior enforcement—arrests away from the border—the criminal share runs the other way, about 93 percent of interior removals in fiscal 2024. The overstay, not the border crossing, has been the larger source of new unauthorized residents since about 2007 by the Center for Migration Studies’ estimates: the Department of Homeland Security counted 538,548 suspected overstay events in fiscal 2024 against 46.7 million expected departures, a rate of 1.15 percent, with Mexico, Colombia, India, and Canada the largest counts and European visa-waiver states contributing about 61,000 suspected overstays against 1,540 European removals in the last full yearbook year. The system holding these cases is backlogged and exposed: 3,037,800 cases pending in immigration court at the end of September 2026 by TRAC’s count, an estimated 1.6 million people on ICE’s non-detained docket carrying final orders, 65,765 people in detention on a July 2026 count of whom 70.6 percent had no criminal conviction, and a resident population of lawful permanent residents whose exposure to the deportability grounds never expires—a conviction from the third year of a forty-year residence is chargeable in the thirty-seventh, because the statute carries no limitations period and only naturalization ends the exposure. The public, polled by Pew and Gallup in 2025, holds a model the statute does not contain—65 percent for a requirements-based path to stay, 97 percent of the selective majority for deporting the violent, 15 percent for deporting the employed—in the language of this report, a ripening doctrine whose only living statutory relative is cancellation of removal’s ten-year presence rule and whose ancestor, the 1986 legalization, has not been rerun; and the precarity the system manufactures is a priced commodity in adjudicated fact, from smuggling fees of $6,500 to $18,000 a person in the sentencing records, through the sanitation contractors’ child-labor judgments, the $14 million Signal verdict, and the $65.5 million au pair settlement, to the lawful tether of the H-1B and the 1.1-million-deep Indian green-card queue. The desk closes the file with the definitions the argument uses loosely—naturalization is a statutory process with stated requirements, not a ripening of residence into entitlement—and with the error file, in which the government’s own auditors have documented citizens arrested, detained, and removed, graded by the same instrument as every other claim in the report.

1. The Legal Architecture: A Civil System with Criminal Edges

Presence is civil; entry is criminal; the distinction organizes the whole system. A noncitizen who is present in the United States without lawful status commits no federal crime by being present. The Supreme Court stated the point in Arizona v. United States, 567 U.S. 387 (2012): “As a general rule, it is not a crime for a removable alien to remain present in the United States.” What the criminal code reaches is conduct at the border and after removal. Improper entry—crossing at an undesignated place, evading inspection, or entering on false documents—is a federal misdemeanor for a first offense under 8 U.S.C. &sect;1325, punishable by up to six months, and a felony on repetition. Reentry after a removal order is a felony under &sect;1326, punishable by up to two years, rising to ten years after removal following certain convictions and twenty years after an aggravated felony. Removal itself—the process the public vocabulary calls deportation—is neither: it is an administrative proceeding conducted by the executive branch, in which the respondent has the right to counsel at no expense to the government, no right to a jury, and a burden structure set by statute rather than by the criminal standard. Since the Illegal Immigration Reform and Immigrant Responsibility Act of 1996, the proceeding has had one name: “removal,” which merged the old exclusion and deportation tracks into a single process under INA &sect;240.

Two lists in the statute book decide who may enter and who must leave, and they are not the same list. INA &sect;212(a) (8 U.S.C. &sect;1182(a)) states the grounds of inadmissibility—the charges applied to a person seeking admission at a port of entry, applying for a visa, or, in specified circumstances, adjusting status or returning from travel. INA &sect;237(a) (8 U.S.C. &sect;1227(a)) states the grounds of deportability—the charges applied to a person who was admitted and is now alleged to have forfeited the admission. The deportability list, which is the operative one for residents, runs in classes: persons inadmissible at the time of entry or adjustment; persons present without admission or parole; persons who violated the conditions of their status, including failure to maintain student or exchange status; persons who fail to register a change of address; document fraud and false claims to citizenship; and the criminal classes at &sect;237(a)(2)—crimes involving moral turpitude, aggravated felonies, high-speed flight, controlled-substance offenses, firearms offenses, and crimes of domestic violence, stalking, and child abuse or neglect. Which list governs a given person is a threshold litigation point in real cases, because the burdens differ: in deportability cases the government must prove alienage and the ground by clear and convincing evidence; in inadmissibility postures the applicant bears more of the burden.
