Verified: established by statute, official record, or adjudication. Documented-but-small: real, proven, and measured against a baseline that bounds its size. Claimed-but-unproven: asserted by named makers, with no instrument at the scale claimed. Disproven: tested by the instrument built to test it and failed.

VerifiedDocumented-but-smallClaimed-but-unprovenDisproven

Unlawful presence is a civil violation, not a crime (Arizona v. United States); improper entry and reentry after removal are crimes (8 U.S.C. &sect;&sect;1325–1326). The ladder runs NTA, hearings, BIA, final order, with expedited, administrative, and reinstatement tracks beside it. A removal order carries 5/10/20-year and permanent bars (&sect;212(a)(9)(A)); voluntary departure carries no removal-order bar. Overstays have exceeded border entries among new unauthorized residents since about 2007 (CMS); 538,548 overstay events were counted in fiscal 2024 (DHS). The Schengen clock is cumulative, 90 in 180, and Switzerland is inside it. The removability grounds contain no character credit; good moral character gates benefits and relief only. A single ordinary DUI is not a deportability ground (Leocal; Lopez-Meza). Deportability has no statute of limitations; only naturalization ends a resident’s exposure. ICE removed 271,484 people in fiscal 2024, 32.7 percent with convictions or pending charges; the interior cut ran 93 percent criminal-involved. Europeans are removed—1,540 in fiscal 2023—under the same statute as everyone else. The public’s model is measured, not guessed: 65 percent for a requirements-based path to stay (Pew, June 2025); of the selective majority, 97 percent for deporting the violent and 15 percent for deporting the employed (Pew, February–March 2025). Precarity is monetized inside the system as a matter of adjudicated record—recruitment debt, confiscated passports, and deportation threats priced by juries and courts in the Signal and Global Horizons cases. The smuggler’s fee is documented in the sentencing record at $6,500 to $18,000 a person, with the unpaid held in stash houses until it was paid (Renoj-Matul, sentenced to 262 months; Mejia-Zuniga, ten years). At the brand-name end of the food and leisure industries, the exploited worker is on a contractor’s payroll, not the brand’s: PSSI, Fayette, Exel, Cal-Clean, HCL, and Cognizant are where the penalties and settlements in the file land.
Wrongful arrests, detentions, and removals of potential citizens: 674 arrested, 121 detained, 70 removed, fiscal 2015–2020, by the GAO’s audit, whose own caveats make the counts floors. European removals: 1,540 of 183,360 formal removals in fiscal 2023, under 1 percent, against about 61,000 European visa-waiver overstays in fiscal 2024. The Abrego Garcia removal: one case, fully documented, error conceded by the agency in court. Deaths in ICE custody: 38 in fiscal 2026, the highest year in the agency’s series, against tens of thousands detained on any given day. Documented voluntary departures: 6,118 court grants in the first six months of 2025—a real channel, at documented scale. Adjudicated exploitation: more than $14 million awarded in David v. Signal International (2015); $8.7 million and $7,658,500 in the Global Horizons cases (2014–2016); 1,558 labor-trafficking situations identified by the national hotline in 2023—floors, built only from cases that reached an authority. The case record of section 14, each item bounded by its instrument: a 54-count indictment of twenty-four defendants and more than $200 million in alleged proceeds in United States v. Patricio, resolved by guilty pleas running from a year and a day for the first-named defendant to thirty years in the related Mendoza case; $1,544,076 in penalties against PSSI for 102 children on overnight sanitation shifts, and $649,304 against Fayette Janitorial for at least twenty-four, with a criminal indictment of Fayette personnel unsealed in 2025 and untried at filing; $164,814 settled by Mar-Jac Poultry after the death of a sixteen-year-old on its sanitation shift, and $385,000 assessed against its Alabama plant for minors as young as thirteen; 188 months for the leader of the Ohio egg-farm ring that held eight Guatemalan minors against their paychecks; New York’s nail-salon task force ordering $2 million to 652 workers in its first year; $213,042 in back wages recovered for 1,028 J-1 students at the Hershey warehouse; and the J-1 au pair sponsors’ $65.5 million settlement in Beltran, paid without adjudication of the wage-fixing alleged.
DHS’s count of 1.6–1.9 million “self-deportations” in 2025: built on survey population estimates, with no published methodology or departure count beneath it. The claim of a million-scale population of unlawfully present Ukrainians and Eastern Europeans: no DHS table at scale supports it; the measured European overstay stock is real and smaller, and most post-2022 Ukrainians hold parole or TPS. The “80 percent” non-criminal share as a constant of the system: no official series states it; the measured series runs 41 percent non-convicted (fiscal 2013) to roughly two-thirds (fiscal 2024) and higher in 2025. The department’s 622,000-deportations claim for 2025 as a figure comparable to the ICE removal series. That elections—or removals—are administered on any basis other than the statutory one, asserted without an instrument: no specimen at scale has been produced in this file, from any direction.
That a single DUI forfeits a green card under current law: Leocal and Lopez-Meza dispose of it; the bill that would make it so, H.R. 875, passed the House in June 2025 and is not law. That criminals are put in deportation facilities instead of jail: the detainer record shows criminal custody and sentence first, ICE custody after. That the border hop resets the Schengen clock: the 90/180 rule is a rolling cumulative window. That “bad hombres” describes the removed population as a whole: the convicted have been a minority of total removals in every recent year of ICE’s published split. That wrongful removal of citizens does not occur: the GAO’s audit is the disposing instrument. That long residence alone ripens into lawful status in the United States: the registry door stands frozen at January 1, 1972, and no other provision enacts the ripening. That an adjudicated record of J-1 or H-2B exploitation by Disney at its parks exists to be cited: the desk’s search of the enforcement and court record finds none—Disney’s documented case is the 2015 replacement of its own American IT staff by a contractor’s H-1B workers, investigated and closed without a violation.

As the file stands on Sunday, November 8, 2026: deportation in the United States is an administrative process built on two statute lists—inadmissibility for those at the door, deportability for those admitted—run through a court track with hearings and appeals and three faster tracks without them, ending in bars of five, ten, and twenty years for the removed, no removal bar for the voluntarily departed, and unlawful-presence bars that turn on time accrued however a person leaves; its recent caseload is majority non-criminal in the totals and majority criminal in the interior, its overstay flow has exceeded its border flow among new arrivals for nearly two decades, its court backlog stands above three million cases, its final orders outstanding above 1.4 million, its detention population near record levels with seven in ten detainees holding no conviction, and its statute asks nothing, at the removability stage, about whether the person before it is good; the resident it holds longest is exposed for the whole of his residence to a list of tripwires that never expire until the oath of naturalization discharges them; the government’s own auditors have documented its errors against citizens at small, real scale; and every large claim in the public argument—the millions self-deported, the eighty percent, the criminal flood, the spotless machine—grades, on the instruments available, below the arithmetic the record actually keeps.

 The File, Clipped

 Everything the desk read for the report above, clipped and filed as a bureau files it. Each item is stamped subjective, a source with a position, printed because it is useful, and described by what it says. The desk’s report is the only part of this file stamped objective. Thirty-one items.

Every section of the desk’s report is a reading of this book.

The spine of sections 4 and 12.

 SubjectiveLeocal v. Ashcroft, 543 U.S. 1 (2004); Matter of Lopez-Meza, 22 I&N Dec. 1188 (BIA 1999); Matter of Castillo-Perez, 27 I&N Dec. 664 (A.G. 2019)The drunk-driving trilogy of section 3: DUI is not a crime of violence and so not an aggravated felony; ordinary DUI is not moral turpitude, though the knowing-unlicensed variant was held to be; two or more DUIs raise a presumption against good moral character. Together they state the current law the pending bill would displace.

 SubjectiveCongress.gov — H.R. 875, the Protect Our Communities from DUIs Act, 119th CongressThe pending text and its path: passed the House June 26, 2025, by 246 to 160; referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee June 27, 2025; no further action recorded at filing. The bill would add DUI—conviction or admission—to both the inadmissibility and deportability lists, without waiver or misdemeanor exception.
